name: Contractual-control agreement preparation tool for conveyancers
demand: There is a real new compliance task: certain development-related rights over registered land must be reported digitally from 6 April 2027; rights granted from 8 June 2026 have a transitional reporting deadline of 6 October 2027, and new or changed rights generally trigger a 60-day deadline. The grantee bears the duty, but an individually regulated conveyancer must submit the information (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-new-reporting-rules-for-contractual-control-rights; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/contractual-control-agreements/contractual-control-agreements). A current third-party count from the SRA firm-data feed lists 3,119 firms reporting commercial-property work as of 20 October 2026; this is a broad, self-reported firm proxy, not a count of firms handling qualifying agreements (https://solicitorcost.com/solicitors; SRA data-service description: https://www.sra.org.uk/datasharing). HMLR says it had engaged around 31 firms and 48 legal professionals in service research by 17 September 2026; that measures research participation, not purchase intent (https://hmlandregistry.blog.gov.uk/2026/09/17/help-shape-our-new-contractual-control-service/). The legislation’s explanatory memorandum estimates £4.2m per annum in business compliance costs, including £3.7m recurring costs and £4.5m one-off familiarisation costs, in 2019 prices; this is a policy cost estimate, not software spend or a serviceable market estimate (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2026/9780348280630/pdfs/ukdsiem_9780348280630_en_001.pdf). Search volume, installs, qualifying agreement counts, active prospective users and willingness to pay are unverified; the memorandum says HMLR will collect submission metadata to estimate prevalence after the service starts (same memorandum URL).
prices: No directly comparable contractual-control preparation product or price found; direct competitor pricing and payment evidence are unverified. HMLR’s existing Digital Registration Service portal is free, but the fee for the new contractual-control service is not stated (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-business-gateway; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-new-reporting-rules-for-contractual-control-rights). As adjacent benchmarks only, Legal CM publishes £12 + VAT per conveyancing completion, £50 + VAT per user per month for non-conveyancing matters, and setup charges of £1,000 + VAT for a starter pack and £400 + VAT per training day (https://www.legalcm.co.uk/). Genie AI publishes £45 per user per month billed annually or £56 month-to-month for its Pro plan (https://www.genieai.co/en-gb/pricing). These are not prices for this specific workflow and do not prove that customers paid.
copy_speed: No exact-match private preparation-tool launch surfaced in this search. Adjacent launches show active competition: RegLand was reported launching on 26 May 2026 as a pre-validation layer for Land Registry applications and offered a limited free pilot (https://thenegotiator.co.uk/news/products-services-news/new-legal-tech-platform-to-end-submit-and-hope-conveyancing/). ClearPathOS launched on 24 August 2026 with broad AI conveyancing and contract-analysis workflows (https://propertysoup.co.uk/clearpath-ai-launches-to-target-conveyancing-overhaul/). HMLR announced its own private beta for November 2026 and a planned April 2027 service launch on 17 September 2026 (https://hmlandregistry.blog.gov.uk/2026/09/17/help-shape-our-new-contractual-control-service/). These are adjacent products or the government service, not verified direct competitors or proof of sales. Inference: once HMLR’s field definitions and submission workflow settle, generic extraction is easy for case-management and legal-AI vendors to copy; clause-level accuracy and workflow integration would take more work.
platform_risk: High. HMLR is building the required submission service, has tested online mapping tools with users, and says the service is in private beta before its planned April 2027 launch; the same product could make simple form preparation unnecessary (https://hmlandregistry.blog.gov.uk/2026/09/17/help-shape-our-new-contractual-control-service/; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-new-reporting-rules-for-contractual-control-rights). HMLR’s October 2026 developer notes add a required contractual-control declaration to certain Land Register APIs, while technical guidance for the separate information-submission service is still forthcoming (https://landregistry.github.io/bg-dev-pack-redesign/support/news/release-notes-2026-10/; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/contractual-control-agreements/contractual-control-agreements). Existing Business Gateway suppliers already connect legal software to HMLR systems, creating potential integration partners and established competitors (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/software-suppliers-integrated-with-business-gateway/software-suppliers-integrated-with-business-gateway). HMLR plans a structured, searchable, reusable public dataset from April 2028, which weakens a moat based only on the submitted fields (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/contractual-control-agreements/contractual-control-agreements).
defensible_asset: Potential, not established: a permissioned corpus of varied agreements with clause-level citations and lawyer-verified field labels; a rules-and-exceptions engine with an audit trail; and integrations that keep matter records and later variations, assignments, exercises and expiries in sync. HMLR’s explanatory memorandum describes variable legal drafting and interpretation difficulty, supporting the need for careful extraction (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2026/9780348280630/pdfs/ukdsiem_9780348280630_en_001.pdf). The core fields and rules are public, and HMLR intends to publish the submitted dataset, so neither the rules nor the submitted data alone are a durable moat (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/contractual-control-agreements/contractual-control-agreements). Switching costs would depend on matter-history and case-management integration; no such asset or customer lock-in exists yet.
build_effort: Unverified; a narrow prototype looks moderate, while a production product is materially harder. The useful MVP is document upload/OCR, structured field extraction with exact clause citations, uncertainty flags, scope/rule checks, lawyer review, and export. HMLR requires machine-readable location data for part-title rights, rejects scanned PDF plans for that purpose, and says the technical submission guidance is still to come (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-new-reporting-rules-for-contractual-control-rights; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/contractual-control-agreements/contractual-control-agreements). Secure handling of confidential agreements and grantor birth details, permissioned training data, auditability, changing HMLR formats, and exception handling add production work. Do not automate the final regulated submission: HMLR requires an individually regulated conveyancer to make it (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-new-reporting-rules-for-contractual-control-rights).
channel: Use a company-branded, inbound-first route: publish a practical compliance checklist and cited sample extraction; seek opt-in distribution through legal-technology suppliers, conveyancing associations, newsletters and webinars; explore Business Gateway integration after HMLR publishes the relevant technical route (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-business-gateway; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/software-suppliers-integrated-with-business-gateway/software-suppliers-integrated-with-business-gateway). HMLR’s private beta is for legal professionals to evaluate its service, not a sales channel (https://hmlandregistry.blog.gov.uk/2026/09/17/help-shape-our-new-contractual-control-service/). Avoid unsolicited electronic marketing to sole traders and certain partnerships: ICO treats them as individual subscribers and says email/text marketing requires consent or a valid soft opt-in; use consented inbound enquiries instead (https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/business-to-business-marketing/).
owner_hours_per_week: Unverified; the <=5 h/week constraint is not demonstrated. It is plausible only with self-serve onboarding, no bespoke legal advice, automated support triage and a stable integration; trust-building, security reviews, exceptions and partner sales could push owner time above the limit. The legally accountable conveyancer still has to review and submit (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-new-reporting-rules-for-contractual-control-rights).
desk_test: Within one working day, make a no-code or spreadsheet mock that turns a sample or synthetic agreement into the published HMLR fields, with every value linked to its source clause and ambiguous fields flagged for lawyer review (field requirements: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/contractual-control-agreements/contractual-control-agreements). Publish it on a company page with an opt-in request for a paid pilot through a relevant professional newsletter or group; do not DM or cold-email individuals. Treat only a paid-pilot commitment from a firm handling development land as a pass; compliments, beta participation and free-trial interest are not payment evidence.
red_flags: No verified revenue or paying customers for this exact product; evidence of payment remains unverified. The duty falls on the grantee, not necessarily the conveyancer who would buy the tool, so buyer and budget ownership need testing (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/contractual-control-agreements/contractual-control-agreements). HMLR will supply the submission service and mapping tools; missing, incorrect or misleading information carries legal consequences, making uncited autonomous outputs unsafe (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-new-reporting-rules-for-contractual-control-rights; https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/contractual-control-agreements/contractual-control-agreements). The SRA firm count is a broad proxy, not a count of qualifying matters. automation_share_pct is 0 to mean unverified, not an estimate that automation is actually zero; the >=50% automation and <=5 h/week constraints remain unproven. Overall: survives the cheap kill-check, but demand, payment, owner-time fit and defensibility are not yet validated.
